title: Comprehensive and reproducible grading of the Updated Sydney System in gastric biopsies using artificial intelligence: multi‐pathologist validation and a reader study

Gastritis is a significant global health concern with clinical implications that extend far beyond transient mucosal irritation. Since specific histological patterns often signal malignant transformation, a thorough evaluation of gastric mucosal injury is essential. The Correa Cascade best articulates this pathological transformation by identifying chronic inflammation as the primary driver of the transition to intestinal‐type gastric adenocarcinoma. 1 , 2 In this model, Helicobacter pylori‐induced inflammation drives a stepwise transition from chronic active gastritis to multifocal atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia (IM), establishing a definitive precancerous environment. 3 , 4 Consequently, accurate and reproducible assessment of gastritis and its premalignant sequelae is essential to enable robust risk stratification and to support evidence‐based treatment decisions. 5 , 6

The Updated Sydney System (USS) provides the histological basis for this assessment and remains the most widely adopted framework for the pathological evaluation of gastritis. 7 The USS itself relies on a semi‐quantitative 0–3 scale encompassing five core histological attributes—mononuclear cell infiltration, neutrophil activity, glandular atrophy, IM and H. pylori density—evaluated across a standardized five‐site biopsy protocol on the gastric mucosa (two antrum, two corpus and one incisura). Based on the USS score, operational staging systems such as Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment (OLGA) and Operative Link on Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia Assessment (OLGIM) formalize this concept by integrating both the severity and topography of atrophy or IM into stage 0–IV categories. In this framework, advanced stages (III–IV) reliably identify high‐risk patients while early stages (0–II) define a low‐risk group, with stages III–IV conferring markedly higher gastric cancer risk than stages 0–II in both OLGA (RR 32.31) and OLGIM (RR 12.38). 8 Since OLGA/OLGIM stages directly depend on the accuracy of these underlying USS scores, precise and reproducible application of the USS is essential for reliable risk stratification and, ultimately, for effective gastric cancer prevention. 9 , 10

Although the USS is the standard framework in routine practice and serves as the histological basis for gastric cancer risk stratification, its consistent application remains challenging because it is inherently limited by the subjectivity of semi‐quantitative visual scoring. While the USS introduces visual analogue scales to standardize grading, true quantification remains difficult. Multiple studies have documented substantial interobserver variability among pathologists, with kappa (κ) values for atrophy and neutrophil activity reported as low as 0.04 and 0.22 in routine practice. 7 , 11 This inconsistency propagates into risk stratification systems, introducing uncertainty into gastric cancer risk assessment and surveillance. Furthermore, the USS imposes a significant diagnostic burden; the standardized five‐site biopsy protocol requires pathologists to examine multiple tissue fragments across all five semi‐quantitative axes, demanding prolonged visual attention and high‐fidelity interpretation.

To address these challenges, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been investigated in histopathology as a potential means of improving the reproducibility and efficiency of gastritis assessment. Early studies, however, mainly focused on narrow tasks, such as H. pylori detection or the separate grading of IM and atrophy. 12 More recent studies have extended this approach to two or three Sydney attributes. 13 , 14 However, in routine gastric biopsy interpretation, these five attributes frequently coexist and are assessed jointly. This creates two important gaps for clinical implementation. First, no previous framework has comprehensively evaluated all five USS attributes within a single model, particularly including H. pylori, which is central to the pathobiology of chronic gastritis. Second, prior studies have often relied on binary or reduced‐category predictions and were developed on relatively modest datasets annotated by a limited number of pathologists. Together, these limitations reduce clinical realism and generalizability, making implementation in routine pathology workflow more difficult.

Here, we developed a unified, weakly supervised multi‐task learning framework that jointly predicts all five Sydney System attributes. We assembled a large‐scale cohort of over 50,000 histologically annotated whole‐slide images (WSIs)—to our knowledge, the largest gastritis dataset to date—capturing the full spectrum of gastric pathology. Further, using an expert‐adjudicated reference dataset, we evaluated whether this approach could support implementation in routine diagnostic workflow.

We retrospectively assembled a large dataset of gastric biopsy specimens from Seegene Medical Foundation (SMF), a high‐volume reference diagnostic pathology laboratory in South Korea. The specimens were obtained between February 2024 and July 2025. They were processed using routine histopathological protocols, including formalin fixation, paraffin embedding, 3 μm microtome sectioning and haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. All slides were digitized at 40× magnification (0.25 μm/pixel) using a Leica Aperio GT450 scanner at SMF.

Each H&E‐stained WSI from gastritis samples was interpreted according to the USS by a single reporting pathologist as part of routine clinical diagnosis. Cumulatively, the retrospective dataset comprised diagnostic labels contributed by multiple board‐certified pathologists. The USS defines five key histological attributes: mononuclear cell infiltration, neutrophil activity, glandular atrophy, IM and H. pylori density. The pathologist‐assigned labels and the AI inputs were derived from the same H&E‐stained WSIs. For H. pylori assessment in this dataset, ancillary special stains or immunohistochemistry (IHC) were not performed, reflecting routine high‐throughput diagnostic practice in which additional stains are not applied to every gastric biopsy. IM was graded according to the USS severity scale irrespective of histological subtype, and SydneyMTL was not trained to distinguish between these subtypes. Each attribute is graded on a four‐point ordinal scale (0 = Absent, 1 = Mild, 2 = Moderate, 3 = Marked). For mononuclear cell infiltration, grade 0 did not indicate complete absence of lamina propria lymphocytes or plasma cells, which may be present in normal gastric mucosa. Rather, it denoted the absence of chronic gastritis beyond the expected physiological inflammatory cell population, according to the USS visual analogue criteria. To ensure high clinical fidelity, we integrated ‘N/A’ (Not Applicable) as a distinct category for glandular atrophy, addressing cases where the absence of the muscularis mucosae precludes definitive grading. By incorporating the full spectrum of labels including ‘N/A’, SydneyMTL better reflects real‐world diagnostic variability and increases robustness to partially evaluable specimens. Unlike previous studies that exclude such cases, our framework explicitly learns these evaluation constraints, mimicking the high‐fidelity decision‐making process of pathologists who must identify non‐evaluable tissue in routine biopsy scenarios. An example of the structured USS report is provided in the Data S1.

In addition, to ensure a rigorous and unbiased evaluation, we created an independent ‘Golden dataset’ (n = 366) collected from a distinct period, which serves as a high‐quality reference standard. For establishing ground truth, three senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience independently reviewed all cases. To resolve interobserver discordance and ensure label reliability, the final ground truths were determined through a multi‐round consensus adjudication process.

sections.title: Unified Multi‐Task MIL Framework for Sydney Grading

paragraphs.en: To perform simultaneous grading of all five USS attributes, we developed a unified multi‐task multiple instance learning framework, SydneyMTL (Figure 1). The model was designed to reflect routine gastric biopsy interpretation, in which a pathologist reviews a WSI and assigns slide‐level grades for multiple histological attributes without requiring region‐level annotations. Because only slide‐level diagnostic labels were available, the model was trained using weak supervision. In this setting, each WSI was treated as a collection of small image patches and the model learned which patches were most informative for each Sydney attribute based only on the final slide‐level grades.

A pretrained pathology feature extractor first converted each patch into a numerical representation of its histological appearance (Figure 1). SydneyMTL then used a shared adapter to compress these patch‐level features into a lower‐dimensional representation that summarized common morphological patterns in gastric biopsies. From this shared representation, separate task‐specific attention modules identified patches relevant to each USS attribute. For example, the H. pylori branch could assign greater attention to regions containing organisms suggestive of H. pylori. The attention‐weighted patch features were combined to generate an attribute‐specific slide‐level representation and separate classifier heads produced the final grade prediction for each attribute. This design enabled simultaneous grading of all five USS attributes while providing attribute‐specific attention maps that indicate which tissue regions contributed most to each prediction.

Routine gastric biopsy datasets are highly imbalanced, with absent or mild findings being much more common than moderate or marked findings. To address this imbalance, we evaluated three optimization strategies: standard cross‐entropy, class‐weighted cross‐entropy and prior‐based logit adjustment. Standard cross‐entropy does not explicitly account for the skewed distribution of USS grades, whereas class‐weighted cross‐entropy increases the training penalty for errors in rare grades. Prior‐based logit adjustment takes a different approach by shifting the model logits according to the empirical class distribution before loss computation. By incorporating the observed prevalence of each grade into the output scores, this method reduces the tendency of the model to favour common grades such as absent or mild findings. 15 Detailed information on WSI preprocessing, patch extraction, feature encoding, model implementation, training procedures and hyperparameter settings is provided in the Data S1.

Model performance was evaluated using stratified fivefold cross‐validation on the retrospective dataset and independent testing on the Golden dataset. Because the USS is ordinal and semi‐quantitative, the primary performance measures were Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) and lenient accuracy. 16 , 17 For lenient accuracy, grade 0 required an exact match, whereas for grades 1–3, predictions within one adjacent category were considered correct provided that they did not cross the boundary between absent and pathological categories. To further examine whether the model preserved the ordinal structure of histological severity, we visualized slide‐level embeddings in a low‐dimensional space. Model interpretability was qualitatively assessed using attention heatmaps and patch‐level feature visualization.

sections.title: Reader Study for AI‐Assisted Diagnostic Workflow Evaluation

paragraphs.en: To evaluate the model's practical utility in real‐world diagnostic workflows, we employed a randomized crossover design. The two review phases were separated by a 5‐week washout period to mitigate recall effects. 18 The order of review conditions was counterbalanced between the two pathologists: one pathologist performed the AI‐assisted review first, whereas the other performed the unassisted review first, with the alternate condition performed in the second phase.

Interobserver agreement was assessed using QWK. Workflow efficiency was evaluated by measuring interpretation time per WSI. The reduction in interpretation time associated with AI assistance was calculated by subtracting the mean AI‐assisted interpretation time from the mean unassisted interpretation time. To assess the statistical significance of this time reduction, linear mixed‐effects models (LMMs) were fitted with review condition as a fixed effect and slide as a random intercept to account for repeated measurements. Statistical significance of fixed effects was assessed using Wald z‐tests. Effect size for efficiency was quantified using Cohen's d for paired samples, reflecting the within‐subject crossover design.

All WSIs used in this study were obtained from SMF, Republic of Korea. These slides were originally collected during routine health checkups and external diagnostic consultations. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Seegene Medical Foundation (No. SMF‐IRB‐2024‐015). All data were fully anonymized prior to analysis, and no identifiable personal information was accessed by the investigators. Given the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de‐identified histological images, the requirement for informed consent was waived by the IRB.

We analysed 50,765 gastric biopsy WSIs in the retrospective dataset. Across the USS attributes, grade distributions were skewed, with absent or lower‐grade categories predominating and high‐grade lesions being relatively uncommon. For example, H. pylori was absent in 78.81% of cases, whereas only 0.53% were graded as marked. Before consensus adjudication, interpathologist agreement in the Golden dataset was variable, with QWK ranging from fair agreement for atrophy (κ = 0.320) to substantial agreement for intestinal metaplasia (κ = 0.667), highlighting the diagnostic difficulty of these features (Table 1). These results underscore the challenge of grading subtle or borderline lesions. 20

sections.title: Comparative Assessment on Retrospective and Golden Cohort

paragraphs.en: When evaluated on the expert‐adjudicated Golden dataset, the logit‐adjusted SydneyMTL model demonstrated statistically significant improvements over standard loss functions in both QWK and lenient accuracy (Figure 2). The largest gain was observed for H. pylori, where SydneyMTL improved the QWK score from 0.592 to 0.826 (p < 0.01) while achieving a lenient accuracy of 95.1%. For IM, SydneyMTL also significantly outperformed the baseline, increasing QWK from 0.796 to 0.898 (p < 0.05). Notably, the benefit of logit adjustment was also evident for glandular atrophy, a highly imbalanced attribute in which nonzero grades, ranging from mild to marked atrophy, accounted for less than 10% of cases. For this task, SydneyMTL improved QWK by more than 0.1 points compared with the CE loss function (0.599 vs. 0.487). These findings suggest that logit adjustment may be more suitable for AI‐assisted USS grading in this imbalanced setting by incorporating the observed prior distribution of USS grades, reducing bias towards common grades such as absent or mild findings, and improving recognition of less frequent but clinically important high‐grade findings.

In contrast, on the retrospective dataset evaluated using fivefold cross‐validation, performance differences between optimization strategies were limited, despite the generally high performance of all optimization strategies. As shown in Figure 2, all approaches closely reproduced the retrospective label distribution and achieved highly saturated performance for several attributes, including H. pylori (lenient accuracy >94% across models), IM, neutrophil activity and mononuclear cell infiltration. Although some pairwise comparisons reached nominal statistical significance in lenient accuracy for specific tasks such as atrophy (p < 0.05), these absolute differences were small and were not consistently reflected in QWK.

sections.title: Robustness of the Model across 24 Individual Pathologists

paragraphs.en: To assess the clinical robustness of our AI model, we evaluated its performance on the retrospective dataset by comparing its predictions against the independent diagnoses of 24 individual pathologists. Overall, SydneyMTL demonstrated strong alignment with the majority of human readers. The model achieved over 80% average lenient accuracy with 21 out of the 24 pathologists and exceeded 90% agreement with a subset of four pathologists (Figure 3). Among the five USS attributes, the model exhibited particularly robust performance for IM and H. pylori. The average lenient accuracy for IM was 93.2%. Similarly, for H. pylori, the model achieved an average lenient accuracy of 93.9% across the 24 pathologists, with a minimum pathologist‐specific lenient accuracy of 83.3%, indicating consistently high‐agreement across different observers. Finally, across all 24 pathologists, the model achieved an average QWK (κ) of 0.734, confirming its high utility as a stable diagnostic aid.

sections.title: AI Impact on Observer Variability and Interpretation Time

paragraphs.en: In the crossover study, AI assistance improved interobserver agreement, with the QWK increasing from 0.751 ± 0.016 in the unassisted setting to 0.774 ± 0.020 with SydneyMTL assistance. The gain was most apparent for diagnostically variable USS attributes, including mononuclear cell infiltration, and was also seen for H. pylori detection. AI assistance was additionally associated with significantly shorter interpretation times (LMM, p < 0.001), corresponding to an overall reduction of 34.3% per WSI. Reader‐specific reductions were 38.7% for pathologist 1 (paired Cohen's d = 0.73) and 29.7% for pathologist 2 (paired Cohen's d = 0.65). These results indicate that SydneyMTL may support more reproducible and efficient application of the USS in routine practice (Figure 4).

sections.title: Preservation of Biological Ordinality in Latent Feature Space

paragraphs.en: To examine whether the model preserved the ordinal nature of the USS grades, we visualized slide‐level embeddings from the Golden dataset using t‐SNE (Figure 5). For key attributes, including H. pylori density, neutrophil activity and IM, the embeddings showed an ordered progression from absent to marked rather than forming unrelated clusters. This pattern was supported by quantitative analysis of distances between grade centroids (Data S1), which increased with greater diagnostic separation. For example, in H. pylori, the distance from the absent centroid increased from 5.88 for mild to 9.15 for moderate and 11.90 for marked cases. These findings suggest that the model captured histological severity as a continuous spectrum rather than as unrelated categories, supporting its clinical plausibility as a grading tool.

We analysed the spatial distribution of attention weights to verify whether the model's decision‐making process aligns with clinically established diagnostic regions. For H. pylori, attention heatmaps were predominantly concentrated on the superficial epithelium (the outer layer of glands) (Figure 6‐Left). Similarly, in cases of IM, the model consistently assigned high‐attention scores to glandular structures containing characteristic goblet cells. Notably, in cases lacking the muscularis mucosae where assessment was precluded, the model appropriately reflected this limitation by categorizing them as ‘N/A’.

To further examine patch‐level representations, we applied principal component analysis (PCA) to patch embeddings and visualized the dominant components. In slides with marked H. pylori, the leading components were localized to small regions containing bacterial aggregates while suppressing background tissue and artefacts (Figure 6‐Right). In IM, one principal component (PC2) preferentially activated mucin‐containing goblet cell regions. For inflammatory features, the dominant components separated morphologically distinct cell patterns, including neutrophils and lymphoplasma cells. These findings indicate that the model based its predictions on histologically meaningful structures rather than irrelevant background signals. For pathologists, this suggssests that the model's outputs are grounded in recognizable microscopic features and may therefore be more trustworthy as a decision‐support tool.

Because H&E examination is less sensitive than ancillary staining for the detection of H. pylori, particularly in cases with mild‐to‐moderate organism density, we performed Giemsa staining to examine whether the model's spatial localization and slide‐level grading corresponded to the ancillary‐stain findings. On H&E‐stained sections, the attention heatmaps highlighted regions along the luminal surfaces and within the lumina of gastric pits and glands (Figure 7). Within these AI‐highlighted regions, H. pylori appeared as scattered individual organisms in mild cases and as progressively denser bacterial aggregates in moderate and marked cases. In these illustrative cases, the corresponding slide‐level predictions were concordant with the reference grades. Examination of spatially matched regions on the Giemsa‐stained sections demonstrated H. pylori at corresponding locations, with organism densities consistent with the respective grades. These findings provide ancillary‐stain support for the histopathological relevance of the model's localization and slide‐level grading.

Accurate histological grading of gastric biopsies is essential for gastric cancer prevention and serves as the basis for risk stratification systems. However, the routine application of the USS is currently hindered by substantial interobserver variability and the labour intensive nature of assessing multiple histological attributes. In this study, we introduce SydneyMTL, the first unified framework capable of simultaneously performing four‐tier grading for all five Sydney System attributes. On the largest cohort of gastric biopsies to date (n = 50,765) and an adjudicated dataset, our model captures the comprehensive histological landscape of chronic gastritis. By automating the grading process with strict adherence to biological ordinality and expert consensus, this work represents a paradigm shift from subjective visual estimation to reproducible, quantitative computational pathology.

In routine pathology workflows, two practical barriers may limit consistent USS reporting. First, USS grading is based on semi‐quantitative visual assessment rather than a strictly quantitative scale, which can contribute to interobserver variability and, consequently, less reproducible downstream gastric cancer risk stratification (OLGA and OLGIM). Second, although chronic gastritis is a non‐neoplastic condition, complete USS reporting requires pathologists to evaluate five histological attributes across four severity tiers, creating a labour‐intensive burden in high‐volume diagnostic settings. In this context, SydneyMTL may contribute to pathology workflows in two complementary ways: by supporting more reproducible histological inputs for risk stratification and by improving efficiency in high‐throughput gastric biopsy interpretation.

For the risk stratification of gastric cancer, gastritis grading is clinically relevant because the histological severity and anatomical distribution of atrophy and intestinal metaplasia are used to stratify gastric cancer risk and guide surveillance decisions. 8 , 20 OLGA and OLGIM stages III–IV identify patients at substantially higher risk of gastric cancer than stages 0–II, with a recent meta‐analysis of prospective cohorts reporting a risk ratio of 32.31 for OLGA and 12.38 for OLGIM. 8 However, the clinical value of these staging systems depends on the accuracy and reproducibility of their histological inputs. 21 , 22 OLGA uses the severity and topography of glandular atrophy, whereas OLGIM uses intestinal metaplasia as a more reproducible histological anchor; both require consistent site‐specific assessment of Sydney‐defined attributes. 20 , 22 This remains challenging in routine practice. SydneyMTL was therefore developed to address this upstream bottleneck: by providing reproducible, task‐specific, and visually interpretable grading of all five USS attributes, the model may help pathologists apply Sydney criteria more consistently and provide a more stable histological basis for downstream OLGA/OLGIM‐based risk assessment. In the reader study, AI‐assisted interpretation with SydneyMTL improved overall mean interobserver agreement from 0.751 to 0.774, even when readers were free to override the model. This finding suggests that the model's initial recommendations may provide a useful clinical reference during USS grading and could be incorporated into routine digital pathology workflows to support more consistent gastric biopsy assessment.

SydneyMTL may also contribute to more efficient diagnostic workflows. Although the generalizability of this workflow analysis is limited by the inclusion of only two pathologists, this reader study demonstrates improved efficiency with AI assistance. This may be particularly relevant in high‐throughput reference laboratory settings, such as those in South Korea, where the National Cancer Screening Programme for Gastric Cancer performed more than 7.8 million screening endoscopies in 2022, with over 2.4 million endoscopic biopsy cases. 23 This screening context generates a large volume of gastric biopsy specimens, most of which show negative findings. Therefore, AI‐assisted USS grading may help reduce the workload associated with high‐volume gastric pathology workflows.

To our knowledge, this is the first reader study to evaluate AI‐assisted workflow efficiency in a setting that closely reflects real‐world comprehensive USS reporting, where pathologists are expected to assess all five histological attributes across four severity tiers while also identifying non‐assessable atrophy. Existing empirical evidence has been limited by the narrower scope of prior studies. Zhou et al. evaluated AI assistance for H. pylori detection alone on H&E‐stained WSIs using IHC‐confirmed ground truth and found that assistance did not reduce overall turnaround time. 24 In contrast, AMMNet demonstrated improved diagnostic efficiency for binary (absent/present) assessment of selected gastritis indicators, including activity, atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, reducing the time required per WSI from 5.46 to 2.85 min, corresponding to a 47.8% reduction; however, its workflow evaluation was limited to binary assessment of selected indicators rather than complete USS grading. 13 Thus, while prior evidence has not been sufficient to establish the workflow value of AI assistance for comprehensive gastritis grading, the present study addresses this gap by evaluating an AI system designed to support the full USS interpretation process used in routine pathology practice. Taken together, these findings suggest that SydneyMTL may support routine digital pathology workflows by providing more reproducible Sydney grading as a histological basis for downstream OLGA/OLGIM‐based risk assessment, while also reducing the workload associated with multi‐attribute gastric biopsy interpretation.

To evaluate the reliability of SydneyMTL, we examined whether its predictions were supported by biologically meaningful histopathological evidence rather than by irrelevant visual cues or spurious correlations. This consideration is particularly important in weakly supervised learning, where models are trained using slide‐level labels and may theoretically exploit non‐diagnostic patterns. We therefore assessed the reliability of SydneyMTL from three complementary perspectives: concordance with expert‐consensus labels and individual pathologist labels, preservation of the ordinal structure of USS grades and localization of model attention to diagnostically relevant microscopic regions.

The model was first evaluated against a Golden dataset established through multi‐round expert consensus, providing a stringent reference standard beyond routine single‐reader labels. This analysis showed that SydneyMTL aligned its predictions with a multi‐expert consensus standard despite being trained on routine diagnostic labels. In addition, across the evaluation involving 24 pathologists, SydneyMTL achieved more than 80% agreement with 21 board‐certified pathologists, indicating that the model's predictions were broadly consistent with routine specialist interpretations rather than being driven by concordance with only a small subset of readers (Figure 3). The >90% agreement observed in a subset of pathologists may partly reflect differences in reader‐specific case volume. Although two of the four high‐agreement pathologists contributed relatively small numbers of WSIs, high concordance was also maintained in two pathologists with larger case volumes. In these higher‐volume readers, SydneyMTL aligned well with pathologist labels in distinguishing absent cases from pathological cases, defined as mild or higher grades. Among pathological cases, most discrepancies were limited to one adjacent severity grade, consistent with the lenient accuracy criterion.

Beyond concordance with expert‐derived labels, the embedding and interpretability analyses provided additional evidence that SydneyMTL captured biologically and histopathologically meaningful patterns rather than relying on non‐specific visual characteristics. In the t‐SNE analysis, slide‐level representations demonstrated a gradual transition from absent to marked grades across most USS attributes. Although partial overlap was observed between adjacent grades, this finding is consistent with the semi‐quantitative nature of histopathological assessment, in which the boundaries between mild, moderate and marked lesions are often continuous rather than sharply demarcated. Importantly, the model largely maintained separation between non‐pathological and pathological categories, suggesting that the learned representations reflected clinically relevant disease states rather than arbitrary distinctions between grading categories.

Previous studies applying deep learning to gastric pathology have primarily addressed interpretability through WSI‐level heatmaps. 13 , 25 , 26 , 27 While these approaches are useful for identifying tissue regions associated with model predictions, they provide limited information regarding whether the underlying image representations correspond to recognizable microscopic structures. This limitation has been acknowledged in prior studies, in which heatmap‐based visualization alone was considered insufficient to fully explain the basis of model decision‐making. 25 In contrast, SydneyMTL extended interpretability beyond simple spatial localization by linking task‐specific attention patterns with histopathologically meaningful image representations. At the patch‐level, PCA‐based visualization further demonstrated associations between dominant image features and specific histopathological findings. Major feature components corresponded to readily recognizable microscopic structures, including aggregates of H. pylori organisms, goblet cell‐rich intestinal metaplasia and characteristic inflammatory cell infiltrates. Accordingly, SydneyMTL did not merely identify broad regions of diagnostic relevance within WSIs but also provided multi‐scale evidence that the morphological features underlying its predictions were aligned with established histopathological criteria. Collectively, concordance with expert assessment, preservation of the ordinal structure of disease severity, and demonstration of histopathologically interpretable image features support the biological plausibility and potential clinical reliability of SydneyMTL as an AI‐assisted framework for USS grading.

Our study has several limitations. First, despite the large‐scale cohort, the data were derived from a single high‐volume centre. Nevertheless, while prior studies typically relied on a limited number of pathologists for evaluation, our study benefits from a more generalizable framework by involving 24 diverse annotators within a single centre. To further ensure generalizability across different diagnostic cultures, external multi‐institutional validation is warranted in future work. The second limitation is that H. pylori density was assessed using H&E‐stained slides only, without systematic confirmation by special stains or IHC. Although this reflects routine high‐throughput diagnostic practice, H&E‐based assessment is less sensitive than ancillary staining, particularly immunohistochemistry, especially in cases with low bacterial burden. Nevertheless, the use of more than 50,000 routine diagnostic cases may reduce the impact of idiosyncratic label noise, and the attention maps showed that high‐attention regions for H. pylori frequently corresponded to morphologically recognizable bacterial colonies, supporting the histological plausibility of the model's predictions (Figure 6). Finally, as this evaluation remains retrospective, we plan to integrate SydneyMTL into the laboratory information system for prospective studies to quantify its real‐world impact on diagnostic efficiency and the reproducibility of gastric cancer risk stratification.

In conclusion, SydneyMTL represents a paradigm shift in gastric pathology as the first unified framework to simultaneously assess all five attributes of the USS. By leveraging an unprecedented large‐scale dataset and adjudicated dataset, the model transcends individual observer bias and aligns with a rigorous multi‐expert consensus. The demonstrated reduction in interpretation time and the harmonization of interobserver variability underscore its potential as a scalable decision‐support tool in high‐volume clinical workflows. SydneyMTL promises to enable standardized, reproducible gastritis grading in routine practice, supporting more timely and accurate gastric cancer risk stratification globally.

figures.caption: Histopathological correlation of H&E‐based AI localization with corresponding Giemsa staining for H. pylori. Illustrative cases selected to demonstrate mild, moderate, and marked H. pylori density are shown. From left to right, the panels present: (1) the whole‐slide H&E image with the AI‐generated attention heatmap, with the selected region of interest indicated by a red box and arrow; (2) the corresponding Giemsa‐stained whole‐slide image with the matched region indicated; (3) the H&E patch extracted from the selected region; (4) the same H&E patch with the AI heatmap overlaid; (5) a digitally enlarged view of the H&E patch; (6) the corresponding Giemsa‐stained patch; and (7) a digitally enlarged view of the Giemsa‐stained patch. Red dashed boxes indicate corresponding areas used for detailed comparison. The spatial correspondence between AI‐highlighted regions on H&E and organisms visualized more clearly on Giemsa staining supports the histopathological relevance of the model's localization.
